items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: A note in a margin that took 358 years to verify
items.claim: Pierre de Fermat wrote in 1637 that he had a proof — too long for the margin — that a to the n + b to the n equals c to the n has no positive-integer solutions for n greater than 2. Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
items.prompt: Why was Fermat's Last Theorem so hard to prove?

options.text: Fermat lied about having a proof — there isn't one

It was eventually shown to be equivalent to a statement about modular forms and elliptic curves (the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture); the modern proof required machinery that didn't exist until the 1980s
Number theorists weren't trying hard enough
It is undecidable in standard axioms

items.reveal_title: Wiles, Frey, Ribet — a chain of insights
items.reveal:
Fermat wrote his marginal note in Diophantus's Arithmetica. Hundreds of mathematicians attempted the proof. Special cases were handled (n = 4 by Fermat himself; n = 3 by Euler; n = 5, 7 in the 1800s).

In 1985, Frey proposed that any non-trivial solution would correspond to an unusual elliptic curve. In 1986, Ribet proved this curve could not be 'modular'. Combined with the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture (all elliptic curves are modular), no solution could exist.

Wiles worked in secret for seven years on Taniyama-Shimura for a key class of elliptic curves. He announced the proof in 1993. A gap was found. With Richard Taylor he repaired it in late 1994. The proof runs over 100 pages and uses 20th-century algebraic geometry that Fermat couldn't have had.

It's almost certain Fermat did not have a real proof. He probably had a flawed attempt for small cases, since he never mentioned the result in subsequent letters.
items.why: Fermat's Last Theorem feels like an elementary statement about integers. Its proof needed centuries of machinery — number theory, algebraic geometry, automorphic forms — that no one in 1637 could have imagined.

items.title: Half the world's billionaires got there partly by luck
items.claim: Repeated coin flips produce some very lucky streaks. The proportion of 'successful' (still in business, in market, alive) entities at the top of a population sample is dominated by selection effects — the unsuccessful disappear from view, leaving the survivors looking exceptional.

options.text: Survivorship bias: we only see the successes, and infer skill from outcomes; randomness alone would have produced some 'winners' from a starting pool, but we don't see the matching losers

items.reveal_title: Survivorship bias and the law of large pools
items.reveal:
If 10,000 hedge fund managers each pick stocks randomly for 10 years, about (1/1024) * 10,000 ≈ 10 will have called the market right 10 years running (by pure luck). These 10 will be on the cover of business magazines, will publish books on their 'secrets', and will attract investor billions.

The other 9,990 are out of business and forgotten.

Mochon and Norton (2011, 2012) replicated this in the lab: random stock-picking among 'subjects' produced 'expert' track records statistically indistinguishable from actual hedge funds. Selection of survivors creates the illusion of skill.

Real-world cases:
- WWII US bombers: aircraft returning from missions had bullet holes in wings and fuselage, not engines or cockpits. The Air Force initially considered reinforcing where the holes were — until Abraham Wald pointed out: planes hit in the engine or cockpit don't return. Reinforce the unhit areas.
- Famous 'success stories' (Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, J.K. Rowling) tell entrepreneurs what to do — but tens of thousands who tried the same things failed.
- Stock market: survivor-bias-corrected returns are ~1-2% per year lower than uncorrected indices, because failed stocks drop out.

The correct statistical question is not 'what did successful X do?' but 'what's the base rate of success among everyone who tried that?'.
items.why: Success seems instructive. Survivorship bias means we systematically learn from outliers and ignore the (invisible) ordinary cases. The math of selection effects is more important than the stories of any individual.
